text.p: Australia coach Terry Venables came under fire on Tuesday over an alleged conflict of interest surrounding the transfer of three local players to English first division side Portsmouth.
Several Australian clubs were poised to make an official complaint over Venables' involvement in the transfers as Portsmouth chairman and owner, the Melbourne Age newspaper said.

National league side Sydney Olympic confirmed that it wanted Soccer Australia to investigate Venables' involvement in the transfers of goalkeeper Zeljko Kalac and midfielders Robert Enes and Hamilton Thorp.

"It appears there is an indirect involvement for Venables in these transfers and we would like Soccer Australia to look into it and take the appropriate action," Olympic president Simon Konstantinidis told Reuters.
Portsmouth bought the trio from Australian clubs for a reported combined fee of A$2.0 million (US$1.52 million).
The dispute has distracted attention from Australia's opening World Cup qualifier against Solomon Islands in Sydney on Wednesday.
Former England coach Venables denied any conflict between his two roles, saying the transfers were handled by Portsmouth manager Terry Fenwick, who travelled to Sydney to sign the trio.
"There is no conflict in me being chairman of Pompey (Portsmouth) and coach of the Australian national side," Venables was quoted as saying in The Age.
"Terry Fenwick has made the decision on these players. I just sent him some (video) tapes of the players and he looked at them. Anyone could have done the same."

Kalac and Enes were named last week by Venables in a 26-man squad for the Oceania qualifying tournament. The Oceania group winners will face a final qualifer against an Asian opponent later this year.

Sydney Olympic president Konstantinidis said the conflict of interest existed because Venables could influence the players' value on the transfer market by selecting them for Australia, who are tipped as likely World Cup finalists.

Venables -- who left his previous job as England manager to concentrate on a variety of legal battles -- would benefit directly if that player was then sold for a higher price to another club in Europe, he said.
Konstantinidis added that the ruling body should uphold an internal inquiry in 1994 into overseas transfers which recommended that the national coach be banned from taking part in negotiations.
David Hill, chairman of Soccer Australia, defended the former England and Barcelona coach, who last year signed a lucrative 19-month contract.
"We don't have any problem with Venables being Portsmouth chairman," Hill said.
"For there to be any conflict of interest, you would have to ask me to accept that Venables would not pick the best available team. I don't accept that proposition," Hill told Reuters.
